{{Short description|German mathematician (1894–1967)}}
'''Roland Percival Sprague''' (11 July 1894, [[Unterliederbach]] – 1 August 1967) was a German mathematician, known for the [[Sprague–Grundy theorem]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ams.org/samplings/feature-column/fcarc-games5 |title=5. Towards a theory for combinatorial games" |website=[[American Mathematical Society]] |accessdate=2017-06-30}}</ref> and for being the first mathematician to find [[Squaring the square#Perfect squared squares|a perfect squared square]].<ref name="squaring.net">{{cite web |url=http://www.squaring.net/history_theory/sprague.html |title=R. P. Sprague |website=squaring.net |author=Stuart Anderson |accessdate=2017-06-30 |quote="R.P. Sprague published his solution to the problem of squaring the square.  Sprague constructed his solution using several copies of various sizes of Z. Moroń's Rectangle I (33x32), Rectangle II (65x47) and a third 12 order simple perfect rectangle and five other elemental squares to create an order 55, compound perfect squared square (CPSS) with side 4205." }}</ref>

==Biography==
With two mathematicians, [[Thomas Bond Sprague]] and [[Hermann Amandus Schwarz]], as grandfathers, Roland Sprague was also a great-grandson of the mathematician [[Ernst Eduard Kummer]] and a great-grandson of the musical instrument maker [[Mendelssohn family|Nathan Mendelssohn]] (1781–1852).<ref name="bmg">{{cite journal|journal=Sitzungsberichte der Berliner Mathematischen Gesellschaft|year=2001|pages=333}}</ref>

After graduation ([[Abitur]]) in 1912 from the Bismarck-Gymnasium in [[Berlin-Wilmersdorf]], Sprague studied from 1912 to 1919 in [[Berlin]] and [[Göttingen]] with an interruption by military service from 1915 to 1918. In 1921 in Berlin he passed the state test for teaching in mathematics, chemistry, and physics. He was Studienassessor (probationary teacher at a secondary school) from 1922 at the Paulsen-Realgymnasium in [[Berlin-Steglitz]] and from 1924 at the Schiller-Gymnasium (temporarily named "Clausewitz-Schule") in [[Berlin-Charlottenburg]], where he became in 1925 [[Studienrat]] (teacher at a secondary school).<ref name="bmg" /><ref>Archivdatenbank der Bibliothek für Bildungsgeschichtliche Forschung: Archivdatenbank der Bibliothek für Bildungsgeschichtliche Forschung: [http://archivdatenbank.bbf.dipf.de/actaproweb/archive.xhtml?id=Vz++++++1e871568-c47e-4cd1-b1b7-09053018d2fa#Vz______1e871568-c47e-4cd1-b1b7-09053018d2fa Documents of Roland Sprague]</ref>

In 1950 Sprague received a PhD under [[Alexander Dinghas]] at the [[Freie Universität Berlin]] with dissertation ''Über die eindeutige Bestimmbarkeit der Elemente einer endlichen Menge durch zweifache Einteilung''.<ref>{{MathGenealogyProject|29799 |name=Roland Sprague}}</ref> At the Pädagogische Hochschule Berlin, Sprague was from 1949 [[Docent|Dozent]], from 1953 Oberstudienrat (senior teacher at a secondary school), and from 1955 Professor.<ref name="bmg" />

Sprague is known for his contributions to [[recreational mathematics]], especially the [[Sprague–Grundy theorem#Development|Sprague–Grundy function]] and its application to [[Combinatorial game theory|combinatorial games]], which Sprague and [[Patrick Michael Grundy]] discovered independently in 1935 and 1939 respectively.<ref>''Über mathematische Kampfspiele''</ref> This result of Sprague's enabled mathematical strategies devised originally by [[Emanuel Lasker]] to be completed,<ref>[[Jörg Bewersdorff]]: ''Glück, Logik und Bluff: Mathematic im Spiel – Methoden, Ergebnisse und Grenzen'', Springer-Spektrum Verlag, 6th edition 2012, {{ISBN|978-3-8348-1923-9}}, [[doi:10.1007/978-3-8348-2319-9]], pp. 120-126.</ref> and provided a method for calculating winning strategies for generalizations of the game of [[Nim]].

==Selected works==
* ''Über mathematische Kampfspiele'', Tôhoku Mathematical Journal, vol. 41 (1935), pp.&nbsp;438–444 ([https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/tmj1911/41/0/41_0_438/_pdf Online-Version]).
* ''Über zwei Abarten von Nim'', Tôhoku Mathematical Journal, vol. 43 (1937), pp.&nbsp;451–454 ([https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/tmj1911/43/0/43_0_351/_pdf Online-Version]).
* ''Unterhaltsame Mathematik : Neue Probleme, überraschende Lösungen'', 2nd edition, 1969.
